a1-greetings:
Say **“Hello”** any time, **“Good morning”** before noon and **“Good evening”** after dark.

Answer “How are you?” with “I am fine, thank you,” and say **“Goodbye”** when you leave.
intro-01:
An introduction has three facts:
- your name
- your work or study
- one thing you like.

Start with **“Hello,”** then say **“My name is …,”** “I study …” or “I work …,” and “I like ….” End with **“Nice to meet you.”**

Short, clear sentences are enough.
a1-alphabet:
Every English letter has a name, like “B” (bee) and “N” (en). A written name starts with a **capital letter**.

To ask for spelling say **“How do you spell it?”** and to hear something again say **“Please repeat that.”**
a1-numbers:
Count with one, two, three. Numbers 13–19 end in **“-teen”** and tens end in **“-ty”**: fourteen is 14 and forty is 40.

Ask **“How many?”** about a count and **“How much?”** about a price.

After one use a singular noun; after two or more use a plural.
a1-dates:
Use:
- **“on”** with days (on Monday)
- **“at”** with clock times (at three)
- **“in”** with months (in March).

Ask about time with “What time is the meeting?”
family-01:
Use **“have”** with I, you, we and they, and **“has”** with he, she and it: “She has a brother.”

Add **’s** to a name to show who someone belongs to: “Lina is Mina’s sister.”

Use **“is”** to describe a person: “My brother is kind.”
a1-home:
Use **“There is”** for one thing and **“There are”** for more than one: “There is a chair. There are two chairs.”

Say **“a”** before a consonant sound and **“an”** before a vowel sound: a table, an orange chair.

Say where things are with “next to.”
routine-01:
Use the **simple present** for daily routines: “I get up at six.” With he, she and it, **add -s**: “She starts at nine.”

After “does” and “does not” use the **base verb**: “Does he work on Sunday?”

Put “usually” before the main verb.
food-01:
Order politely with **“I would like tea, please”** or **“Can I have a sandwich?”** Ask a price with **“How much is the sandwich?”**

Use **“some”** with things you can’t count, like water. Add -es to make “sandwiches.”
a1-shopping:
Ask the price with **“How much is this?”** For more than one thing say **“How much are these?”**

Use **“it”** for one thing and **“them”** for more than one: “I will take it. I will take them.”

Say “too big” when a size doesn’t fit.
a1-places:
Start a question about a place with **“Where is …?”** Give directions with the **base verb**: “Turn left. Go straight.”

Use **“next to”** for a place beside another place, and start politely with **“Excuse me.”**
a1-hobbies:
Say what you like with **“I like …”** and what you play with **“I play …”** With he, she and it, add -s: “She likes music.”

After **“can”** use the base verb: “She can swim.”

Join opposite ideas with **“but.”**
a1-weather:
Describe the weather with **“It is …”**: “It is cold. It is sunny.”

For something happening now use **“is raining.”** For a habit use **“rains”**: “It rains a lot in winter.”

Ask **“What is the weather like?”** and take “a coat” when it is cold.
a2-travel:
Use the **past simple** to talk about a finished trip: “I went to Boston last year.” Many common verbs are **irregular**:
- go becomes went
- take becomes took.

Use **“because”** to give a reason and **“so”** to give a result.

Say when with “last year,” “in June” or “two days ago.”
a2-transport:
Ask for directions with **“How do I get to…?”** and **“Where is the…?”** Use the past simple for what happened: “I missed the bus.”

Use **“next”** for the one that follows: “the next train.”

Say how you travel with:
- “by bus,”
- “by train”
- “on foot.”
a2-appointments:
To book a visit, say **“I would like to book an appointment.”** To change it, say **“I need to reschedule.”**

Ask “Is Thursday available?” and use **“Could I…?”** to ask politely for a time: “Could I come at two?”

Use “on” with days and “at” with clock times.
a2-health:
Describe a problem with **“I have a sore throat”** or **“My head hurts.”**

Use **“since”** with a starting point (since Monday) and **“for”** with a length of time (for three days).

Give advice with **“should”**: “You should rest.” Say “I feel ill” when you are sick.
a2-eating:
At a restaurant, say **“A table for two, please.”** Ask politely: **“Could we see the menu?”**

Use **“so”** for a result: “The soup was cold, so I asked again.”

Say **“I would recommend the fish”** to suggest something, and ask for “the check” when you finish.
a2-invitations:
To invite someone, say **“Would you like to come?”** or **“Are you free on Saturday?”**

To say no politely, say “I’m busy on Sunday, but maybe next week.”

Use **“Let’s”** to suggest a plan: “Let’s meet at six.” Thank the person for asking.
a2-leisure:
Talk about last night with the **past simple**: “We saw a movie.”

Use **“too”** for a problem with a limit (too tired, too crowded) and **“enough”** for the right amount (enough time).

Use **“after”** to say what came next: “We walked after the movie.”
a2-work:
Describe your day with **“usually”** for habits and the **past simple** for what happened: “Yesterday I stayed late.”

Say what was necessary with **“had to”**: “I had to finish the report.”

Use **“while”** for two things at the same time: “I answered calls while she was out.”
a2-past:
Use the **present perfect** for life experience: “I have never tried skiing.” Use the **past simple** when you say when: “I went swimming last summer.”

Ask “When did you go?” for the time.

**“Already”** means before now: “She has already seen that movie.”
a2-plans:
Use **“be going to”** for plans you have already made: “I am going to visit my uncle.” Use **“will”** for a decision at the moment: “I will call him tonight.”

Say when with “next month,” “tonight” or “in July.” **“Planning to”** also shows an intention.
a2-problems:
To explain a problem, use the **past simple** for what happened: “I locked my keys in the car.” Use **“so”** for a result: “The elevator was broken, so I walked.”

Ask for help politely: **“Could you help me?”**

Describe the state of a thing with an adjective: “My phone is broken.”
b1-education:
Use **“used to”** for a past habit or state that is no longer true: “I used to study law.”

Use **“because”** to give a reason and **“harder than”** to compare. Talk about decisions with **“I decided to…”**

A course is a set of classes on one subject.
b1-career:
Talk about goals with **“I hope to…”** and **“I would like to…”** Use **“so”** to give a purpose: “I am studying so I can apply.”

Use the **present perfect continuous** for something that began in the past and goes on: “I have been keeping a record.”

You apply for a job or a course.
b1-relationships:
Use the **present perfect** with **“since”** for a starting point (since college) and **“for”** for a length of time (for two years).

**“Although”** shows a contrast: “We argue, although we listen.”

Use **“each other”** when two people do the same thing to one another.
b1-technology:
**“Which is why”** gives the result of what you just said: “My phone died, which is why I wrote.”

Use **“during”** with an event (during the call) and **“instead of”** for a replacement (an app instead of a notebook).

**“You had better”** gives strong advice: “You had better write it down.”
b1-entertainment:
Compare with **“longer than”** or **“better than.”** Say what you prefer with **“I would rather…”**: “I would rather watch a short series.”

**“Worthwhile”** means worth your time.

**“While”** joins two ideas that are true at the same time: “The story is slow while the acting is strong.”
b1-culture:
Describe customs with **“usually”** and **“are expected to”**: “Guests usually bring a gift. People are expected to arrive early.”

Use **“whereas”** to contrast two things: “Work is strict, whereas home is flexible.”

**“Such as”** introduces examples.
b1-community:
**“Who”** joins a sentence to the people you describe: “The neighbors who joined now talk.”

Use **“so that”** to give a purpose: “We did it so that the park would stay open.”

Use the **present perfect** for experience: “They have never organized an event.”
b1-achievements:
Use **“after”** with an **-ing verb**: “I passed after failing twice.” **“Finally”** shows the end of a long effort.

Use the **past perfect** for an earlier past: “I was proud after I had failed.”

Say you are **“proud of”** the result.
b1-decisions:
Explain a decision with **“I chose…”** and **“because”**: “I chose the smaller apartment because it was closer.”

**“Too”** means more than is good: “It was too far.”

Use **“rather than”** to name the choice you did not make: “I picked evening rather than morning.”
b1-unexpected:
Describe a surprise with the **past simple**: “The train stopped between stations.”

**“By the time”** means before a point in the past: “By the time I arrived, it had started.” **“Ended up”** shows an unplanned result: “I ended up taking a taxi.”

Use **“between”** for two places.
b2-projects:
Report a problem with **“slipped by”**: “The launch slipped by two weeks.”

**“Would rather… than”** states a preference: “I would rather delay than ship it.” **“Even though”** admits a fact that points the other way: “Even though we had a date, we waited.”

A **blocking bug** stops users from finishing a task.
b2-leadership:
A lead **“invites dissent”** early: they ask for disagreement before a decision.

**“Even when”** names a condition that does not change the action: “She decides even when the group is split.”

**“Rather than”** names what you avoid. **“Is responsible for”** means you own the result.
b2-media:
**“Imply”** means to suggest something without saying it: “The headline implied a cause.” Use **“who”** for people: “Readers who stopped at the headline were misled.”

**“Never proved”** says it was not shown at all.

**“As if”** compares with something that is not true: “It reads as if the clip were the event.”
b2-social:
Use **cause verbs** to describe an effect: “Higher rent pushes workers outward.” **“Farther”** compares distance: “They live farther from work than before.”

**“While”** can mean at the same time as: “Build the line while protecting residents.”

Use **“who”** for the people you protect.
b2-innovation:
Describe a useful change by saying what it was and what it was not: “The change was not the tool itself. It was the removal of a step.”

Use **“that”** to link a step to its description.

**“Rather than”** names the option you did not choose: “removal rather than another screen.”
b2-ethics:
Use **“if”** for a condition: “If we collect it only because we can, we should stop.” Use **“unless”** for “except if”: “Do not keep it unless there is a named use.”

“We have not earned the right” uses the **present perfect**.

**“Owe”** means to have a duty to give: “We owe users an explanation.”
b2-environment:
Compare results with **“more than”** and **“better than”**: “The thermostat cut more energy than the cups did.”

Use **“by”** for the size of a change: “by two days.”

**“Rather than”** says which option you choose over another: “Choose the default rather than the campaign.”
b2-present:
Open a presentation by **stating the decision** you want before the history: “I am asking you to approve the plan.” Then give facts that support it.

Use:
- **“then”** to show order,
- **“by” plus an -ing verb** to show the method (close by naming the ask),
- **“before”** to set a limit.
b2-negotiation:
Offer **one trade at a time**.

Use **“if”** for a condition: “We can move the date if the scope stays fixed.” **“As long as”** also sets a limit: “We can extend it as long as the list stays still.”

Say **“both”** for two things together and **“neither”** for no side: “Neither side can defend that.”
b2-disagree:
Disagree and still own the result. “Although I see the risk, I choose the trial.”

**“Still”** shows you keep your choice: “I still choose the short trial.” Use **“if”** for what you will accept: “I will own it if it fails.”

Use **“while”** to join two true things: “We can disagree while staying respectful.”
c1-strategy:
Test a plan against **real capacity**, not only against the slide.
- “The plan looks efficient on a slide” uses **“looks”** for appearance.
- **“Frays when…”** shows when a plan breaks.
- “People who must carry it” names who does the work.
- **“Rather than”** prefers one option: “Sequence the work rather than announce a transformation.”
c1-research:
A **cautious claim** stays inside its evidence. “The sample supports a cautious claim,” but it **“does not license a general rule.”**

Use **“may”** for possibility: “Missing answers may tilt the result.”

“Although the interviews agree, the claim stays local” admits a point and still limits the claim. To **tilt** a result is to push it one way.
c1-change:
People often resist the surprise of a change more than the change itself. Say **“not so much the process as the surprise.”**

**“Without practice”** names what is missing. **“Before”** sets an order: “Let them try it before you retire the old way.”

Use **“who”** for people: “Those who missed the reason struggle.”
c1-problems:
Separate tangled causes by **naming each one**: “The handoff is unclear, and the team has no time.”
- **“Only”** limits: “Fixing only the form will fail.”
- **“Both”** joins two sides: “It disappoints both sides.”
- **“Unless”** means “if not”: “Nothing improves unless the receiver has time.”
c1-policy:
A rule people can use puts its **exception next to it**. “A rule that takes longer than a minute will be avoided.”
- **“Or”** warns about the other path: “Write it down, or people will invent a path.”
- **“Beside”** means next to.
- **“Will”** predicts: “The workaround will become the practice.”
c1-sensitive:
To raise a sensitive issue, describe the **pattern and its effect** without turning it into a trial: “Name the effect without putting you on trial.”

“When the meeting runs over, the notes pile up.”

**“So that”** gives the purpose: “Say it so that they can answer the work.”
c1-debate:
To locate a disagreement, separate the **aim** from the **measure**. “The fight is not about the goal. It is about which evidence counts.”

Use **“when”** for the moment of conflict and **“whereas”** to contrast two groups: “One group trusts the survey, whereas the other trusts the log.”
c1-culture:
Do not translate silence into agreement. Ask what a pause means before you fill it.

“What a pause means” is an **indirect question**: use **normal word order** after “what.”

**“Rather than”** names the habit to avoid: “Wait rather than treating silence as agreement.”
c2-abstract:
A **distinction** separates two ideas that are often mixed. “Privacy is a claim about who decides the boundary; secrecy can be that claim, or it can be a refusal to let a decision be seen.”

**“Less… than…”** compares: “Freedom is less the absence of limits than the choice of limits.”

**“Worth keeping”** means deserving to be kept.
c2-interpret:
Hold **more than one reading** of the same words. A pause can read as respect, doubt or refusal.

“The sentence does not decide” its own meaning; “the history does the work.” Use **“or”** to list possibilities.

A neat reading may feel decisive and still be wrong.
c2-debate:
**Grant a point** and still **refuse the leap**. “I can grant the strongest version of your case and still reject the leap, because the step is untested.”

“Agreement on the facts is not agreement on the conclusion.”

Use **“still”** to show that you keep your position.
c2-culture:
A **cultural reference** can fail when the room does not share the story.
- “The joke lands only if the room shares the story.”
- “The story it points at may be missing.”
- “Explaining it spends the laugh.”
- “She would rather be understood than impressive.”

Translate the point into **plain speech**.
c2-multi:
Hold a problem **across fields** without blurring them. “One sees a constraint, one a risk, and one a year of tradeoffs.”

A fix for only one view will fail. “Averaging them is not a synthesis.”

Use **“only”** to mark the limit and **“will”** to state the result.
